gloss: The flat ledge at the bottom of a window or door frame.
examples: The cat spends all afternoon asleep on the *sill*.
She lines up her herb pots along the kitchen *sill*.
Water had rotted the wooden *sills* on the north side.

gloss: A craftsperson who makes and repairs objects out of silver.
examples: Paul Revere worked as a *silversmith* before the Revolution.
A local *silversmith* repaired the broken teapot handle.
Two *silversmiths* had booths at the craft fair.

gloss: A way in which two things are alike.
examples: There is a strong *similarity* between the two paintings.
The detective noticed *similarities* in the three cases.
Any *similarity* to real people is purely coincidental.

gloss: The quality of being easy to understand or free of unnecessary parts.
examples: I love the *simplicity* of this recipe.
The design wins people over with its *simplicity*.
For the sake of *simplicity*, let's assume the rate stays the same.

gloss: A model or exercise that imitates a real situation so it can be studied or practiced.
examples: The pilots ran a landing *simulation* twice a week.
Computer *simulations* predict a much warmer decade.
The whole hospital took part in a disaster *simulation*.

gloss: A machine that reproduces the conditions of driving, flying, or operating something, for training.
examples: He logged forty hours in the flight *simulator*.
The driving school just bought two new *simulators*.
You can crash the *simulator* without hurting anyone.

gloss: The quality of being honest and really meaning what you say.
examples: Nobody doubted the *sincerity* of her apology.
He said it with such *sincerity* that the room went quiet.
The jury questioned the witness's *sincerity*.

gloss: A hole in the ground formed when the surface suddenly collapses into a space below.
examples: A *sinkhole* swallowed half the parking lot overnight.
Florida gets more *sinkholes* than any other state.
They closed the road until the *sinkhole* was filled in.

gloss: A polite way of addressing a man, especially one whose name you do not know.
examples: Can I get you anything else, *sir*?
*Sir*, you'll have to step out of the vehicle.
The letter opened with "Dear *Sirs*".

gloss: A feeling of loyalty and support among women.
examples: There was a real sense of *sisterhood* in that locker room.
The book celebrates *sisterhood* across generations.
She found *sisterhood* in her neighborhood book club.

gloss: A single continuous period spent doing one thing without getting up.
examples: I read the whole novel in one *sitting*.
The restaurant serves dinner in two *sittings*.
The portrait took four *sittings* to finish.

gloss: The set of conditions that exist at a particular time.
examples: We're in a difficult *situation* with the landlord.
The manager handled the *situation* well.
These *situations* come up more often than you'd think.

gloss: Someone who rides a skateboard.
examples: A *skateboarder* nearly ran into me on the sidewalk.
The plaza is full of *skateboarders* after school.
She's the best *skateboarder* in her age group.

gloss: Someone who doubts claims that other people accept.
examples: I was a *skeptic* until I tried it myself.
The results convinced even the *skeptics* on the committee.
He's a lifelong *skeptic* about diet fads.
contrast: Americans spell it *skeptic*; the British spell it *sceptic*.

gloss: A book of blank pages used for drawing.
examples: She carries a *sketchbook* everywhere she goes.
His old *sketchbooks* are full of half-finished faces.
I bought a small *sketchbook* for the trip.

gloss: Someone who jumps from an aircraft and falls freely before opening a parachute.
examples: The *skydiver* landed right on the target.
Six *skydivers* linked hands in the air.
My uncle is an experienced *skydiver*.

gloss: The sport of jumping from an aircraft and free-falling before opening a parachute.
examples: *Skydiving* is on my bucket list.
He took up *skydiving* after he retired.
Her insurance doesn't cover *skydiving*.

gloss: The loose part of a rope, or spare room in a schedule or workload.
examples: Pull in the *slack* before you tie the knot.
Cut him some *slack* — it's only his second day.
When she left, the rest of us picked up the *slack*.

gloss: Someone who avoids work or effort.
examples: He has a reputation as a *slacker*, but the work gets done.
The coach has no patience for *slackers*.
I felt like a *slacker* next to my roommate.

gloss: Casual dress pants that are not part of a suit.
examples: He wore gray *slacks* and a blue shirt.
I need a new pair of *slacks* for the interview.
Her *slacks* were still at the dry cleaner's.
contrast: *Slacks* is always plural; one item is *a pair of slacks*.

gloss: A skiing or boating race down a zigzag course marked by poles or gates.
examples: She won the women's *slalom* by half a second.
The giant *slalom* is scheduled for Tuesday.
Both *slaloms* were postponed because of fog.
contrast: The first syllable sounds like *ah*: SLAH-lum, not SLAY-lom.

gloss: A false spoken statement that damages someone's reputation.
examples: He threatened to sue the station for *slander*.
Calling her a thief on the radio was plain *slander*.
The case turned on whether the remark counted as *slander*.
contrast: *Slander* is spoken; the written form is *libel*.

gloss: A sloping angle, or a particular bias in how information is presented.
examples: Cut the stems at a *slant* before you put them in water.
Every network gave the story a different *slant*.
The roof has a steep *slant* on the back side.

gloss: A hit with the open hand.
examples: She gave him a *slap* across the face.
He greeted me with a friendly *slap* on the back.
A few *slaps* on the lid loosened the jar.

gloss: Comedy based on clumsy physical action such as falls and chases.
examples: The movie is pure *slapstick* from start to finish.
Kids love *slapstick* more than clever dialogue.
There's a long tradition of *slapstick* in silent film.

gloss: The killing of animals for meat, or the violent killing of many people.
examples: The cattle were shipped off for *slaughter*.
The report describes the *slaughter* of an entire village.
New rules govern how *slaughter* is carried out.
contrast: Despite the spelling it is not *laughter* with an s: say SLAW-tur, rhyming with *water*.

gloss: The act of walking around while still asleep.
examples: *Sleepwalking* runs in his family.
The doctor asked whether the *sleepwalking* had gotten worse.
We put a gate on the stairs because of her *sleepwalking*.

gloss: A control that you move along a track to change a setting.
examples: Drag the *slider* to adjust the brightness.
The app has *sliders* for bass and treble.
Move the *slider* all the way to the left to mute it.

gloss: A Y-shaped stick with an elastic band, used to shoot small stones.
examples: He made a *slingshot* out of a forked branch.
The kids were firing acorns from a *slingshot*.
The store stopped selling *slingshots* years ago.

gloss: A small piece of paper, often a printed form or a receipt.
examples: Fill out the deposit *slip* before you get in line.
She handed me a *slip* with her number on it.
Keep your parking *slips* for reimbursement.

gloss: A long narrow cut or opening.
examples: The skirt has a *slit* up the back.
He watched the street through a *slit* in the blinds.
Cut two small *slits* in the top of the pie.

gloss: Someone who is lazy and messy.
examples: My roommate is a total *slob*.
I felt like a *slob* in sweatpants at the fancy brunch.
The house was shared by four cheerful *slobs*.

gloss: A narrow opening for putting something in, or a reserved place in a schedule.
examples: Drop the coin in the *slot* and press the button.
I got the last appointment *slot* on Friday.
The show moved to a better time *slot*.

gloss: A reduction in speed, activity, or economic growth.
examples: Economists are predicting a *slowdown* next year.
There was a major *slowdown* on the interstate.
Seasonal *slowdowns* always hit the store in January.

gloss: A sudden or prolonged fall in sales, prices, or performance.
examples: Housing prices are in a *slump*.
The team is trying to snap out of a hitting *slump*.
Two straight *slumps* forced the company to cut staff.

gloss: An insulting word or remark, especially about someone's race, religion, or group.
examples: He was fired for using a racial *slur* on air.
The report counted dozens of *slurs* in the chat logs.
She refused to repeat the *slur* in court.

gloss: A severe infectious disease, now eradicated, that caused fever and permanent scars.
examples: *Smallpox* was declared eradicated in 1980.
My grandfather still had *smallpox* scars on his arm.
The vaccine against *smallpox* was the first of its kind.

gloss: A small self-satisfied or mocking smile.
examples: He answered with an infuriating *smirk*.
Wipe that *smirk* off your face.
The camera caught a few *smirks* in the back row.

gloss: Someone who smokes tobacco regularly.
examples: He was a heavy *smoker* for thirty years.
The hotel has no rooms for *smokers*.
As a former *smoker*, she notices the smell right away.

gloss: A buffet of many different dishes, or by extension a wide variety of anything.
examples: The hotel laid out a *smorgasbord* for the holiday.
The catalog offers a *smorgasbord* of course options.
Their potlucks turn into enormous *smorgasbords*.

gloss: Someone who moves goods or people across a border illegally.
examples: The *smuggler* was caught at the border crossing.
*Smugglers* used the tunnel for almost a year.
He paid a *smuggler* to get his family out.

gloss: A quick informal photograph, or a brief picture of how things stand.
examples: I found an old *snapshot* of my parents at the beach.
The survey gives a *snapshot* of what voters think today.
She keeps *snapshots* of the kids taped to her monitor.

gloss: A facial expression or remark showing scorn.
examples: He looked at my old car with a *sneer*.
There was a *sneer* in her voice when she said it.
The article was full of *sneers* at small-town life.

gloss: Someone who looks down on people they consider less refined or important.
examples: Don't be such a coffee *snob*.
He's a *snob* about anything that isn't imported.
The club was full of *snobs* in expensive shoes.

gloss: The attitude of looking down on people considered inferior.
examples: There's a lot of *snobbery* in the wine world.
Her *snobbery* about public schools annoyed everyone.
The review dismissed the show with obvious *snobbery*.

gloss: Swimming near the surface with a mask and a breathing tube.
examples: We went *snorkeling* off the south shore.
The resort rents gear for *snorkeling*.
*Snorkeling* is easier to learn than scuba diving.
contrast: American English writes one l, *snorkeling*; British English doubles it, *snorkelling*.

gloss: Someone who rides down snow slopes on a snowboard.
examples: A *snowboarder* cut right in front of me on the run.
Most of the *snowboarders* head straight for the half-pipe.
She's the youngest *snowboarder* on the national team.

gloss: The sport of riding down snow-covered slopes on a single board.
examples: *Snowboarding* became an Olympic sport in 1998.
He gave up skiing for *snowboarding* in college.
The resort offers *snowboarding* lessons for beginners.

gloss: A deliberate act of ignoring or slighting someone.
examples: Not inviting her was a clear *snub*.
The nomination *snub* was all anyone talked about.
He shrugged off the *snubs* and kept working.

gloss: The state of not being drunk, or of staying away from alcohol and drugs.
examples: He's celebrating five years of *sobriety*.
The officer gave her a field *sobriety* test.
The program supports long-term *sobriety*.

gloss: Someone who believes the community or state should own and control major industries.
examples: He ran for mayor as a democratic *socialist*.
The *socialists* won a majority in the last election.
She calls herself a *socialist* but votes pragmatically.

gloss: Someone with no conscience or concern for other people's feelings.
examples: The prosecutor called him a cold *sociopath*.
Movies love to write villains as *sociopaths*.
Not every rude coworker is a *sociopath*.

gloss: A liquid added to laundry to make fabric feel soft.
examples: Add the *softener* to the little middle compartment.
I skip the *softener* on towels.
This *softener* has no added fragrance.
contrast: The t is silent, as in *soften*: SAW-fuh-nur.

gloss: Comfort felt at a time of sadness or trouble.
examples: She found *solace* in long walks by the river.
There was little *solace* in the doctor's answer.
Music was his only *solace* that winter.

gloss: A card game played alone.
examples: He plays *solitaire* on his phone during layovers.
My grandmother taught me *solitaire* on rainy days.
A game of *solitaire* takes about five minutes.
contrast: British English usually calls this card game *patience*.

gloss: A movement in which you roll your body forward or backward in a complete circle.
examples: She did a *somersault* on the living room rug.
The diver managed two *somersaults* before the water.
He landed the backward *somersault* perfectly.
contrast: The o in the first syllable sounds like the u in *sun*: SUM-ur-sawlt.

gloss: A system that uses sound waves to find objects under water.
examples: The submarine showed up on *sonar* just after midnight.
Fishing boats use *sonar* to locate schools of fish.
*Sonar* mapped the whole floor of the bay.

gloss: A poem of fourteen lines with a fixed rhyme scheme.
examples: We had to memorize a Shakespearean *sonnet*.
He wrote her a *sonnet* for their anniversary.
Her collection includes forty *sonnets*.

gloss: An image of the inside of the body produced by sound waves.
examples: They showed us the *sonogram* at twelve weeks.
She keeps the first *sonogram* in her wallet.
The *sonograms* showed everything was normal.

gloss: A man in stories who uses magic powers.
examples: The *sorcerer* turned the prince into a crow.
Two *sorcerers* fought over the same spellbook.
He plays a *sorcerer* in the new fantasy series.

gloss: The use of magic powers, especially evil ones.
examples: The villagers accused her of *sorcery*.
The whole plot turns on a piece of ancient *sorcery*.
In the story, *sorcery* always demands a price.

gloss: A social organization of women students at an American college.
examples: She joined a *sorority* her freshman year.
The *sorority* raised money for the food bank.
There are nine *sororities* on campus.

gloss: A type or category of person or thing.
examples: What *sort* of music do you like?
He's not the *sort* to complain.
The store carries all *sorts* of imported cheese.

gloss: Bread, or the live starter it is made from, raised by naturally occurring yeast.
examples: I feed my *sourdough* starter every morning.
We had grilled cheese on *sourdough*.
San Francisco is famous for its *sourdough*.
contrast: The gh is silent: the second half sounds exactly like *doe*.

gloss: The direction to your left when you face the sunset, or the region lying that way.
examples: The birds head *south* every October.
Their farm is ten miles to the *south*.
She grew up in the *south* of the state.

gloss: The direction or region halfway between south and east.
examples: The storm is moving toward the *southeast*.
Most of the rain falls in the *southeast*.
Take the highway and head *southeast* for an hour.

gloss: Someone from the southern part of a country.
examples: As a *southerner*, he takes his iced tea sweet.
Plenty of *southerners* have moved to the city.
You can tell she's a *southerner* the moment she speaks.
contrast: The first syllable is not like *south*: say SUTH-, with the vowel of *sun*.

gloss: The direction or region halfway between south and west.
examples: The wind was coming out of the *southwest*.
Cactus grows all over the *southwest*.
Their cabin is in the *southwest* corner of the county.

gloss: A king, queen, or other supreme ruler of a country.
examples: The oath is sworn to the *sovereign*, not the government.
Several European *sovereigns* attended the funeral.
She was crowned *sovereign* at the age of nineteen.
contrast: The g is silent and the word has two syllables: SAHV-run.

gloss: The bean used to make sauce, milk, tofu, and oil, or products made from it.
examples: I take my coffee with *soy* instead of milk.
Add a splash of *soy* sauce at the end.
The county exports mostly corn and *soy*.

gloss: A sealed pressurized suit that lets a person survive outside a spacecraft.
examples: It takes hours to get into a *spacesuit*.
The museum has two original *spacesuits* on display.
A tear in the *spacesuit* would be fatal.

gloss: A sudden involuntary tightening of a muscle.
examples: A *spasm* in my back woke me up at three.
The medication reduced the *spasms* considerably.
He gets a *spasm* in his calf whenever he runs.
contrast: The -sm ending is two syllables: SPAZ-um, not one-syllable SPAZM.

gloss: A phone setting or device that plays the call aloud so you can talk hands-free.
examples: Hang on, you're on *speakerphone*.
He drives with the phone on *speakerphone*.
The conference room has two *speakerphones*.

gloss: A common variety of mint used in gum, tea, and cooking.
examples: She always has a pack of *spearmint* gum in her bag.
The tea smells strongly of *spearmint*.
I planted *spearmint* along the back fence.

gloss: An impressive or shocking sight or public display.
examples: The fireworks were quite a *spectacle*.
He got drunk and made a *spectacle* of himself.
The parade is one of the great *spectacles* of the year.

gloss: Guessing about something without firm evidence.
examples: There's a lot of *speculation* about who will get the job.
The company refused to comment on *speculation*.
That's pure *speculation* at this point.

gloss: Someone whose job is to write speeches for another person to deliver.
examples: She worked as a *speechwriter* for two governors.
The president's *speechwriters* stayed up all night.
A good *speechwriter* learns to imitate the boss's voice.

gloss: A set of words believed to have magic power.
examples: The witch put a *spell* on the whole village.
He learns three new *spells* in the second book.
Only true love could break the *spell*.

gloss: The male reproductive cells, or the fluid containing them.
examples: The clinic screens every *sperm* donor carefully.
*Sperm* counts have been falling for decades.
The egg is fertilized by a single *sperm*.

gloss: A mythical creature with a lion's body and a human head, or a statue of one.
examples: The *sphinx* asked every traveler the same riddle.
A row of stone *sphinxes* lined the temple road.
She sat there like a *sphinx*, giving nothing away.
contrast: The ph is said as /f/, so the word begins SF-: SFINKS.
